description: InCir "Innovation Circle" is a five-person team from Abasyn University, Peshawar. We are building AgroShift for Field Shift: a crop-rotation decision-support platform for Peshawar Valley. It combines NASA POWER climate context with crop, soil, water, and calendar data to compare rotation scenarios. Skills: software engineering, frontend/backend, AI/ML, data analysis, Earth science, agriculture, visualization. Decision support only; no yield or profit guarantees.
summary:
AgroShift is a climate-aware crop-rotation decision-support web app for farmers and advisors in Peshawar Valley, Charsadda and Mardan. Farmers pin their farm on a map, choose their current crop and a goal (for example water conservation), either by tapping or by voice in Urdu or English. AgroShift then runs a NASA-data “farm checkup” and compares three transparent rotation plans side by side: a baseline, a water-saver pulse rotation and a soil-shield forage rotation. Each plan shows its seasonal schedule, water-demand indicator, soil-health score, NASA evidence, risks and assumptions, and can be downloaded as PDF or CSV.

It addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA Earth-observation data (POWER, SMAP/Crop-CASMA, GPM IMERG and MODIS/VIIRS NDVI) into simple choices that help farmers adapt to heat waves, irregular rainfall and canal-water gaps. It matters because farmers face high-stakes decisions with little accessible information. AgroShift is honest about its limits. Data is gridded, missing observations are never interpolated, and no yields are guaranteed. Local verification is always advised.
details:
What it does. The farmer pins a location, picks a crop and goal, and AgroShift evaluates four NASA-derived signals:

  • NASA POWER (primary engine): daily climate, heat stress ≥35°C, frost ≤2°C and growing degree days.
  • SMAP L4 / Crop-CASMA: root-zone soil moisture, flagging irrigation deficit below 25 mm/m.
  • GPM IMERG: satellite rainfall, flagging dry-spell risk at 14+ consecutive dry days.
  • MODIS/VIIRS NDVI: vegetation greenness, flagging a bare-fallow window when NDVI is below 0.25.

Rules map these signals to three candidate rotations: A) Current Baseline (Wheat → Maize → Fallow), B) Water-Saver Pulse Fix (Wheat → Mung Bean → Chickpea/Millet) and C) Soil-Shield Forage (Berseem → Hybrid Maize → Cowpea). Each plan shows its evidence, risks and assumptions, and exports to PDF or CSV.

Why it’s useful. Peshawar Valley farmers face irregular canal turns (Warabandi gaps) that push them toward costly diesel tube-wells, heat waves that bake bare soil between wheat and maize, and nitrogen depletion from cereal-after-cereal rotations. AgroShift gives them and extension workers a clear starting point with no technical expertise needed.

Creativity and design choices. The app is built for accessibility, with a map-first interface and Urdu/English voice input. Every recommendation is traceable to its NASA evidence. Satellite gaps remain visible as gaps. The app states the grid resolution of each source (POWER 0.5°×0.625°, SMAP ~9 km, IMERG ~10 km), says that rotations are candidate scenarios rather than guarantees, and prompts users to check canal schedules, seed prices, salinity and pest pressure locally before planting.

Tools. Next.js, FastAPI, Leaflet, Recharts, SQLite, NASA POWER API, SMAP/Crop-CASMA, GPM IMERG, MODIS/VIIRS NDVI. Deployed on GitHub Pages.

Next steps. Add local crop and soil knowledge, partner with agricultural extension services, improve offline access and Urdu voice support, and expand to more districts and crops.
